parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *IKEA *is a well-known home furniture retailer with stores throughout the world. It was started in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad when he was given some money by his father for doing well at school. He wanted to produce furniture at a price that people could afford to buy.
> 
> He realised that transporting furniture to customers was difficult as goods were often damaged. He developed flat packs to avoid damage. A flat pack contained all the materials needed to self-assemble a table, a chair or a bed.
> 
> All *IKEA *stores are run as franchises.

A Canadian supplier of timber charges *IKEA *\$19.75 Canadian Dollars (CAD) per load.

The exchange rate is \$1 CAD = 6.58 Swedish Krona (SEK).

Which **one **of the following would be the cost to IKEA for 1,000 loads in Swedish Krona?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is D — 129 955.00 SEK**

The cost in CAD for 1,000 loads is:

$19 . 75 \times 1  000 = 19  750  \text{CAD}$

Converting to SEK:

$19  750 \times 6 . 58 = 129  955 . 00  \text{SEK}$

**A** is incorrect as it divides only the number of loads by the exchange rate: $1  000 \div 6 . 58 = 151 . 98  \text{SEK}$

**B** is incorrect as it divides by the exchange rate instead of multiplying: $19 . 75 \times 1  000 \div 6 . 58 = 3  001 . 52  \text{SEK}$

**C** is incorrect as it calculates the total cost in CAD but does not convert to SEK: $19 . 75 \times 1  000 = 19  750 . 00  \text{SEK}$

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *The Better Toy Store (TBTS)* is a children’s toy shop. *TBTS *has three shops in Singapore. Two of the shops are located in busy shopping malls and the third is located at the Jewel Changi Airport. *TBTS *has a website for customers looking to buy toys online.
> 
> *TBTS *selects toys to sell that are excellent for play, value, design and quality. All *TBTS *toys are environmentally friendly.

*TBTS *sells balloons in packs of four at a price of 67.60 SGD. 
The exchange rate is 1 SGD = 3.05 Malaysian Ringgit (MYR).

Which **one **of the following would a customer in Malaysia pay in MYR for 4 balloon packs?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is D – 206.18 MYR**

The cost of 4 balloon packs in SGD:

$4 \times 67 . 60 = 67 . 60  \text{SGD}$

Converting to MYR:

$67 . 60 \times 3 . 05 = 206 . 18  \text{MYR}$

**A** is incorrect as it is the price of one balloon pack divided by 4, i.e. $67 . 60 \div 4 = 16 . 90$

**B** is incorrect as it is the price of four balloon packs in Singapore Dollars divided by 3.05, i.e. $67 . 60 \div 3 . 05 = 22 . 16$

**C** is incorrect as it is simply the price of one pack of four balloons in SGD, not converted to MYR

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *NEXT *is a well-known clothing retailer that operates in 70 countries and employs over 43,000 employees. Since *NEXT *commenced trading it has introduced many other products to its range such as home interiors, flowers and a wedding list service.
> 
> In 1999 *NEXT* launched its own online shopping platform, enabling customers to purchase its products where ever they live. It continues to improve its customer service by introducing new initiatives such as next day delivery.
> 
> *NEXT* mainly uses its own factories for production. However, it does purchase some clothes such as ladies dresses from Turkish factories.

*NEXT *purchased 5,000 dresses from a Turkish manufacturer at 101.10 New Turkish Lira (TRY) per dress.

The exchange rate is £1.00 (GBP) = 6.74 (TRY)

Which **one **of the following would *NEXT *pay in £ (GBP) to the Turkish manufacturer for the 5,000 dresses?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is D**

The total cost in TRY is:

$5 , 000 \times 101 . 10 = 505 , 500  \text{TRY}$

Converting to GBP:

$505 , 500 \div 6 . 74 = 75 , 000  \text{GBP}$

**A** is incorrect as 5,101 is calculated by adding 5,000 + 101.10

**B** is incorrect as 5,674 is calculated by adding 5,000 + (100 × 6.74)

**C** is incorrect as 33,700 is calculated by multiplying 5,000 × 6.74

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *Artify Studio* was set up in 2015 by Tay Hui Jae in the busy Kampong Glam area of Singapore.* Artify Studio*’s aim is to have ‘a communal art space where people can come together and paint, where people would be given as much creative freedom as they would have if they were in their own spaces.’
> 
> *Artify Studio* provides many services including its popular Liberty Art Jam where customers can paint as well as listen to music. The studio offers a Corporate Art Jam and Regular Kids Classes. Customers can purchase art materials after attending the studio.
> 
> *Artify Studio* is a profit-making organisation with a social element. It employs seven part-time people, all of whom are art enthusiasts.

*Artify Studio* imports sets of acrylic paint from Malaysia at a cost of 8.50 Malaysian Ringgit (MYR) per set.

The exchange rate is 1 MYR = 0.33 S\$ (SGD).

Which **one **of the following would *Artify Studio* pay in SGD if they imported 15 sets of paints?

Select **one **answer
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is D**

The cost of 15 sets of paint in MYR:

$15 \times 8 . 50 = 127 . 50  \text{MYR}$

Converting to SGD:

\$\$127.50 \times 0.33 = 42.08\,\text{S\\$}\$\$

**A** is incorrect as this is the result of dividing the cost of one set (8.50 MYR) by the number of sets (15) and then multiplying by the exchange rate, or a similar miscalculation

**B** is incorrect as this only converts the cost of one set of paint into SGD without accounting for the 15 sets ($8 . 50 \times 0 . 33 = 2 . 81$), then possibly applying a further error

**C** is incorrect as this is simply the number of sets ordered, ignoring the cost and exchange rate calculation

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *The Alternative Drum School (TADS) *was set up in the wealthy area of Cricklade, England in 2008 by Ollie Tanner who had a passion for and enjoyed drumming. Ollie invested all of his savings into the drumming school. He saw the potential of being located away from other drumming schools.
> 
> Ollie promotes his business by writing columns in local papers, performing at local music festivals and by word of mouth recommendations. He has invested heavily in computer technology to allow students to produce the music they enjoy playing.
> 
> Ollie finds it difficult to maintain a good work-life balance. Ollie currently works 60 hours a week in a business that does not have reliable profits.

*TADS *has developed contracts with drumming schools in other countries to teach online music lessons.

An Italian drumming school has agreed that *TADS* can teach five lessons per week. Each lesson costs £15 for half an hour. The exchange rate in January 2019 was £1 = €1.15.

What will the Italian drumming school pay in euros (€) for these five lessons?

Select **one** answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is D**

The total cost in GBP is:

$5 \times 15 = 75  \text{GBP}$

Converting to euros:

$75 \times 1 . 15 = 86 . 25  \text{EUR}$

The Italian drumming school will pay EUR86.25 for the five lessons.

**A** is incorrect as this is worked out by multiplying five lessons by the exchange rate of EUR1.15

**B** is incorrect as this is simply the cost of one lesson in GBP, not converted to euros

**C** is incorrect as this is worked out by multiplying the cost of each lesson at GBP15 by five lessons, without converting to euros

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]** > Saha is a small business in Türkiye (formerly known as Turkey) that opened in 2020 with 15 employees. It designs and manufactures robots which are used in hospitals, hotels and restaurants. In hospitals its robots are used to move medical supplies between departments. In hotels and restaurants, the robots are used to welcome customers as they arrive and deliver food and drinks to hotel rooms and restaurant tables. > > Saha provides a seven-day-a-week customer service for all businesses buying its robots. Many new businesses are entering the global robot market and are competing for market share. Competitors in Türkiye include NIO, Zoox and Vention. > > Saha has ambitious growth plans and has started to design robots that will be used in the home to help people with cleaning, shopping, security and entertainment. It aims to become a multinational business within five years to manufacture robots in all continents of the world > > **Figure 3 **is an extract from *Saha*’s statement of financial position. > > | | TRY

(million) | > |---|---| > | Current assets | 12 | > | Inventory | 4 | > | Current liabilities | 7 | > > **Figure 3** Analyse the benefits for *Saha *of becoming a multinational business.
parts.solution_md:
By manufacturing robots in all continents of the world, Saha would be able to sell its products to a much larger global market **[1 mark]**. This is important because many new competitors such as NIO, Zoox and Vention are entering the robot market in Türkiye  **[1 mark]**, so expanding internationally would allow Saha to find new customers and increase revenue beyond its increasingly competitive home market **[1 mark]**

Becoming a multinational would also allow Saha to manufacture robots closer to its customers in different countries **[1 mark]**. This would reduce the cost of transporting robots to hospitals, hotels and restaurants in those regions **[1 mark]**, helping Saha to offer competitive prices and grow its market share as it launches its new range of home robots for cleaning, shopping, security and entertainment **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying benefits for Saha of becoming a multinational business
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the benefits to Saha's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefits to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Manufacturing in different countries could give Saha access to cheaper labour and lower production costs **[1 mark]**. This would help the business to compete on price against rivals like NIO, Zoox and Vention **[1 mark]**, which is important as more businesses are entering the global robot market and competing for market share **[1 mark]**
> - Operating across multiple continents would allow Saha to spread its risk across different economies **[1 mark]**. If demand for robots falls in one region, sales in other continents could compensate **[1 mark]**, giving the business more financial stability as it pursues its ambitious growth plans **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that list six benefits for Saha of becoming a multinational business with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> As We Grow (AWG) is a clothing business in Iceland. The social objective of the business is to use natural materials, such as wool, and produce environmentally friendly products. It aims to design clothes that will last a long time, to encourage families to buy fewer clothes and reduce waste in society.
> 
> AWG’s increasing product range now includes jumpers, dresses, shirts and baby clothes. These are produced in small workshops that employ family and friends. Waste is kept to a minimum and any leftover material is used to make scarves and hats.
> 
> The business has one store in Iceland. It uses its website to advertise and sell its clothing online to customers in other countries. The business has received the Icelandic Design Award for its contribution to the environment.
> 
> *AWG *is an importer and an exporter. It imports materials to make its jumpers and exports its clothing to international customers.

Analyse the impact on *AWG *of a depreciation of the ISK.
parts.solution_md:
A depreciation of the ISK means that AWG's imported materials, such as wool, will become more expensive to buy from foreign suppliers** [1 mark]**. This will increase AWG's production costs for its jumpers, dresses, shirts and baby clothes **[1 mark]**, which could reduce profit margins unless AWG raises its prices, potentially putting off the families it aims to serve **[1 mark]**

However, a weaker ISK also means that AWG's clothing will become cheaper for international customers to buy **[1 mark]**. This could increase demand from overseas customers who purchase through AWG's website **[1 mark]**, helping to boost export sales and revenue, which is important for a business that only has one store in Iceland and relies on online sales to reach customers in other countries **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying impacts on AWG of a depreciation of the ISK
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the impacts to AWG's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the impacts to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Higher import costs may force AWG to look for cheaper alternative materials **[1 mark]**. However, AWG's social objective is to use natural materials like wool **[1 mark]**, so switching to cheaper alternatives could compromise its environmental values and damage the reputation that earned it the Icelandic Design Award **[1 mark]**
> - Increased export sales from the weaker ISK could give AWG the revenue needed to expand its product range further **[1 mark]**. With more income from international customers, AWG could invest in developing new products from leftover materials **[1 mark]**, supporting its aim of reducing waste while growing the business beyond its single store in Iceland **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that list six impacts on AWG of a depreciation of the ISK with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone

The exchange rate was \$1 = 6.70 CNY (Chinese Yuan Renminbi)

Calculate the cost of this smartphone in US Dollars. You are advised to show your working.
parts.solution_md:
**\$798.96**** [2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for correctly substituting numbers into the formula
> 
> Award full marks for the correct numerical answer without working
> 
> **Calculation steps**
> 
> Divide the CNY cost by the dollar exchange rate
> 
> $=5,353\div6.70\,\,=798.96$     **[1 mark]**
> 
> Express the answer in US dollars

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Vento is a bicycle manufacturer based in Milan, Italy. It employs 85 workers and exports 70% of its bicycles to countries outside the European Union (EU), including the USA, Japan and Australia. Vento imports lightweight aluminium from China to keep productin costs low. In the past year, the euro has appreciated significantly against the US dollar, Japanese yen and Australian dollar, but has depreciated against the Chinese yuan.
> 
> Vento's owner, Marco, is concerned about the impact of these exchange rate changes on the business. He is considering whether to start manufacturing in one of Vento's export markets to reduce the business's exposure to exchange rate fluctuations.

Evaluate the impact of the exchange rate changes on Vento. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solution_md:
An exchange rate is the value of one currency expressed in terms of another currency. When a currency appreciates, it increases in value compared to other currencies **[K]**

The appreciation of the euro against the US dollar, Japanese yen and Australian dollar means that Vento's bicycles will become more expensive for customers in these countries to buy** [K]**. Since Vento exports 70% of its bicycles to the USA, Japan and Australia** [Ap]**, this could lead to a significant fall in demand as customers switch to cheaper competitors, reducing Vento's sales revenue at a time when these export markets make up the majority of its business **[An]**

However, the euro has depreciated against the Chinese yuan, which means that the aluminium Vento imports from China will become more expensive **[K]**.** **This will increase Vento's production costs for its lightweight bicycles **[Ap]**, squeezing profit margins from both sides as the business faces higher costs and potentially lower export revenue at the same time **[An]**

Overall, the exchange rate changes are likely to have a seriously negative impact on Vento **[E]**. The business is highly exposed because it relies on exports for 70% of its sales and imports its key raw material from China **[Ap]**. Marco's idea of manufacturing in an export market could help to reduce this exposure in the long term, as selling in local currency would remove the exchange rate risk on exports **[E]**. However, this would require significant investment that may be difficult to fund when profits are already being squeezed** [Ap]**. In the short term, Vento may need to absorb some of the cost increases and accept lower profit margins to keep its prices competitive and retain customers in the USA, Japan and Australia** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - The stronger euro could force Vento to lower its prices in export markets to remain competitive → this would reduce profit margins on 70% of its sales → potentially threatening the financial viability of the business
> - Vento could try to find alternative suppliers of aluminium in countries where the euro has not depreciated → this would help to control production costs → although the quality may not match the lightweight Chinese aluminium that Vento currently uses
> - The exchange rate changes may encourage Marco to focus more on selling within the EU where there is no currency risk → reducing Vento's dependence on exports to the USA, Japan and Australia → although this would mean entering new markets where the business may not have an established customer base
> - If the exchange rate changes are temporary, Vento may be better off absorbing the short-term impact rather than making costly long-term changes like relocating production → maintaining its current operations and customer relationships → until the euro returns to a more favourable level

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Solis is a solar panel manufacturer based in Porto, Portugal. It employs 120 workers and sells its products across Europe. Two years ago, Solis began exporting to countries in Africa, where demand for solar energy is growing rapidly. Solis currently manufactures all of its products in its single factory in Porto.
> 
> The African Union has recently formed a new trade bloc that removes tariffs on goods traded between its member countries. Solis is not based within this trade bloc. Several of Solis's competitors have already opened factories in Africa to take advantage of the trade bloc. Solis's owner, Carla, is considering whether to open a factory in a member country of the African trade bloc to remain competitive.

Evaluate whether Solis should open a factory within the African trade bloc. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solution_md:
A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers, such as tariffs, between them **[K]**

Opening a factory within the African trade bloc would allow Solis to sell its solar panels to member countries without paying tariffs** [K]**. This is important because several competitors have already opened factories inside the bloc **[Ap]**, so if Solis continues to export from Porto it will face higher costs than its rivals, making its solar panels more expensive and less competitive in a market where demand is growing rapidly **[An]**

However, opening a factory in Africa would require significant investment in land, equipment and training new workers** [K]**. Solis currently manufactures all of its products in a single factory in Porto with 120 employees** [Ap]**, so Carla has no experience of managing operations across two continents, which could stretch the business's resources and lead to problems with quality control or production delays** [An]**

Overall, Solis should open a factory within the African trade bloc** [E]**. Demand for solar energy in Africa is growing rapidly, and competitors are already establishing themselves inside the bloc **[Ap]**. If Solis does not act, it risks being locked out of this growing market by tariffs that make its products too expensive compared to those manufactured within the bloc **[An]**. While the investment is significant, the cost of doing nothing could be greater, as Solis would watch competitors take market share that it may never be able to win back **[E]**. Carla could start with a small factory to limit the initial investment and scale up as the business establishes itself in the African market** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - A factory in Africa would bring Solis closer to its customers in the region → reducing transport costs for heavy solar panels that currently have to be shipped from Porto → helping to lower prices and increase competitiveness
> - Solis could benefit from lower labour costs in some African countries → reducing its overall production costs compared to manufacturing in Portugal → increasing profit margins or allowing it to offer more competitive pricing
> - Carla may struggle to find workers with the specialist skills needed to manufacture solar panels → training a new workforce takes time and money → and production quality may initially be lower than at the established Porto factory
> - Opening a second factory means Solis would be operating in a different legal and regulatory environment → Carla would need to understand local laws on employment, tax and manufacturing standards → which adds complexity and cost to running the business

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Wave is a surfboard manufacturer based in Peniche, Portugal. It was set up six years ago by Tomás and employs 20 workers. Wave sells its handcrafted surfboards to surf shops across Europe. The business has built a strong reputation for high-quality boards, and Tomás takes pride in personally overseeing every stage of production.
> 
> Tomás has noticed that demand for surfboards is growing rapidly in South America, particularly in Brazil. Brazil is a member of the Mercosur trade bloc, which removes tariffs on goods traded between its member countries. Wave currently pays a 15% tariff on all surfboards exported to Brazil.

Tomás is considering two options to grow sales in South America:

- Option 1: Continue exporting surfboards from Portugal to Brazil and absorb the 15% tariff.
- Option 2: Open a small factory in Brazil to manufacture surfboards within the Mercosur trade bloc.

Justify which one of these two options Wave should choose
parts.solution_md:
A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers, such as tariffs, between them. A tariff is a tax placed on imported goods, which increases the price for the buyer** [K]**

Continuing to export from Portugal means Tomás can maintain full control over the quality of every surfboard **[K]**. He currently oversees every stage of production personally** [Ap]**, so staying in Peniche ensures the high-quality reputation that Wave has built over six years is protected, which is what attracts surf shops across Europe** [An]**

However, the 15% tariff makes Wave's surfboards more expensive for Brazilian customers** [K]**. As demand for surfboards is growing rapidly in Brazil **[Ap]**, Wave risks losing potential sales to competitors who can manufacture within Mercosur and sell without the tariff, making it difficult for Wave to compete on price in this growing market** [An]**

Opening a factory in Brazil would allow Wave to sell surfboards within Mercosur without paying the 15% tariff** [K]**. This would make Wave's prices more competitive in Brazil and across other Mercosur member countries **[Ap]**, helping the business to take advantage of the rapidly growing South American market and significantly increase its customer base beyond Europe **[An]**

The drawback is that opening a factory in Brazil requires significant investment, and Tomás would be managing production across two continents** [K]**. With only 20 employees currently in Peniche, the business may not have the resources or experience to set up operations in a new country **[Ap]**. Tomás would also be unable to personally oversee production in Brazil, which could lead to a drop in quality that damages Wave's reputation **[An]**

Wave should choose Option 1 **[E]**. The business's strongest asset is its reputation for high-quality handcrafted surfboards, built over six years under Tomás's personal oversight **[Ap]**. Opening a factory in Brazil risks compromising this quality and stretching a small business too thin. While the 15% tariff increases costs, Wave could pass some of this on to customers who are willing to pay a premium for a high-quality European-made board **[Ap]**, rather than risking the brand on a factory Tomás cannot directly control** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Exporting from Portugal means Wave does not need to invest large sums in a new factory → keeping costs low and the business financially secure → which is important for a small business with only 20 employees
> - The 15% tariff may become unsustainable if competitors within Mercosur offer similar quality surfboards at lower prices → Wave could gradually lose its share of the growing Brazilian market → missing the opportunity to establish itself before the market becomes saturated
> - A Brazilian factory would bring Wave closer to its South American customers → reducing shipping costs for bulky surfboards that currently travel from Portugal → and allowing faster delivery times which could improve customer satisfaction
> - Tomás may struggle to find skilled craftspeople in Brazil who can match the quality of his handcrafted boards → training new workers takes time and the results may be inconsistent → which could lead to customer complaints and damage the reputation Wave has built across Europe
